title: Federation over Harness
summary: Modern LLM-powered agents increasingly improve through experience sharing, where distributed agents distill local reasoning experience into reusable knowledge, such as a shared insight library. Existing approaches, however, still heavily rely on manually designed prompts and workflows that determine both how local agents extract useful reasoning traces and how a central/global agent aggregates them to obtain common patterns and insights. We propose Federation over Harness (FoH), a framework that automatically evolves the harness for both local and global components in this distributed multi-agent reasoning pipeline. A server agent evolves the client harness for task solving and self-reflection while, at the same time, evolving its own harness for aggregating distributed reflections, maintaining shared knowledge, and updating subsequent client harnesses. Importantly, FoH requires no extra validation signals, such as ground-truth labels or validation data, during evolution; it learns solely from self-generated reflections produced by distributed agents. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that FoH consistently improves over single-agent baselines with a fixed harness and with harness self-evolution by 53.57% and 29.76%.

title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
summary: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.

title: The Weight of Teamwork: Does Communication Structure Help LLM Scientists Search for Scientific Laws?
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundations of Agentic Systems Theory (FAST), non-archival. 7 pages main text, 33 pages total with appendices
summary: Team performance is often reported as one delivered score, even though that score is produced in two stages: a system generates candidate answers and a selection rule returns one of them. We use symbolic regression as an observable scientific-search setting and compare fixed-budget LLM teams that differ in peer visibility and update timing, evaluating both their frozen candidate archives and the expressions selected from those archives. Distributing the call budget across more independent trajectories produced the largest measured gain, improving mean held-out fitting score Q by 0.70 at the widest tested allocation. Under a common archive-wide selector, the implemented Ring policy reduced mean Q by 0.33 relative to Independent, while Star and Complete remained unresolved. Holding the generated archives fixed, changing the delivery rule changed the measured architecture gaps, including the sign of the Complete point estimate. These results support reporting candidate generation and final selection as separate endpoints. They do not identify a communication mechanism or a universally preferred topology; rather, they show that an architecture ranking is not identified by communication structure alone when the rule that returns the final answer is left unspecified.

title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Model Capacity Frontier} (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

title: From Prefabricated Content to Situated Generation: A Four-Wave Longitudinal Study of AI-Mediated Museum Surfaces and Spaces
comment: ACM ISS 2026 PACMHCI full paper; revised manuscript; 5 figures; 3 tables; accepted paper
summary: Generative AI changes a basic condition of interactive surfaces and spaces (ISS): visitor-facing content can be produced during interaction rather than fully authored before it. We report a longitudinal qualitative study with 23 Chinese science museum practitioners, interviewed annually from 2023 to 2026 (retention 23 to 19) and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants' accounts moved from anticipated epistemic and operational risks, through backstage experimentation and visitor-facing trials, toward situated governance and renewed questions about the purpose of museum interaction. Following these changes over time shows how generative AI reconfigured the design problems of museum ISS: generated content appeared under institutional authority; inference delay became publicly and bodily experienced; concurrent touch, gesture, and speech created ambiguous multi-user intent; and post-generation editing could leave curators selecting within an AI-defined possibility space. We conceptualize the resulting shift as a movement from prefabricated display to situated generation and formulate four design propositions concerning provenance at the point of display, spatially appropriate fallback, multi-intent negotiation, and curatorial control before generation. These propositions are grounded in practitioner accounts rather than evaluations of implemented solutions.

title: Measuring the Influence of Modality-Specific Node Representations on Graphs
summary: Multimodal attributed graphs combine graph structure with node text and image representations in recommendation and multimedia analysis. Graph predictors propagate these representations across connected nodes, so one input can change predictions at its own and nearby nodes. Measuring this distributed response reveals which modality-specific inputs a trained model relies on and how predictor design changes that reliance. We study influence measurement for modality-specific node representations. Given an encoded graph, a trained predictor, a training split, and fixed candidate representations, the task outputs one influence score per candidate and separate text and image rankings. We score a candidate by replacing it with its modality's training-node mean and comparing the original and changed predictions. Existing feature attribution and data valuation generally target one output, training examples, whole nodes, or graph elements rather than prediction changes across graph nodes. Our empirical study shows that nearby-node responses contain information missed by source-only scores and simple proxies, while response magnitude alone does not identify which class changes support the task. Guided by these observations, we propose MoGI (Modality-specific Graph Influence). It propagates training labels to define task direction, reads the same replacement response for the favored class and full class distribution, and averages the resulting ranks. MoGI requires no predictor retraining or learned scoring parameters. Under a shared five-dataset, eight-predictor benchmark, it achieves the largest aggregate held-out loss increase against all five external methods at every tested ranking cutoff.

title: From Critical Transitions to Sustainability Transformations: Phenomena, Theory, and Applications Across Disciplines
summary: There has been a recent surge in the use of terms describing systemic change processes across science, policy, and public debate. The associated change phenomena are often assumed to be abrupt and irreversible once critical thresholds are crossed. However, the interchangeable use of terms leaves definitions and the underpinning scientific theory unclear, which can lead to misconceptions about transition processes and potential impacts. Here, we present selected empirical examples representing phenomena of tipping points, regime shifts, critical transitions, phase transitions, social and socio-technical transitions, and sustainability transformations, together with their underlying theory derived from the broadly defined domains of physics and mathematics, Earth science and ecology, social sciences, and their interdisciplinary overlaps. We bring these fields into closer conversation, creating a shared understanding of each of the conceptual roots, phenomena, mechanisms, and specific applications. This can help steward the governance of social-ecological change towards more just and sustainable futures.

title: ROAR: Benchmarking LMM Agents under Real-Time Constraints in Multiplayer Action-Shooter Games
summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that perceive, reason, and act in interactive multi-agent environments. Yet most existing benchmarks for LMM-based agents in multi-agent settings remain turn-based: the environment and other agents pause while an agent performs inference. Such protocols obscure a fundamental challenge of real-time constraints, where the world continues to evolve and delayed decisions may become outdated before execution. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce ROAR, a multiplayer action-shooter game environment for evaluating LMM-based agents in multi-agent settings under real-time constraints. ROAR covers cooperative, competitive, mixed cooperative-competitive, and basic single-agent scenarios. We further propose a Multi-Agent Asynchronous Gym interface that decouples environment evolution from agent reasoning by running the environment and each agent in separate threads, enabling the environment to advance at fixed time intervals without waiting for LMM inference and allowing agents to reason independently without blocking one another. ROAR also features convenient deployment, multimodal observations, and customizable levels. ROAR offers a practical testbed for advancing LMM-based agents beyond static, turn-based evaluation toward real-time multi-agent decision-making.

title: Over reliant and underprepared: First responder resilience to disruption of operational technology
summary: The Emergency Services Sector (ESS) is responsible for taking life-saving action in the face of extreme crises. To enhance its response capabilities, the sector has spent the last two decades investing in new technology to improve their operational efficiency. This has created significant interdependencies and a culture among first responders of technical overreliance, raising questions about what would occur if those tools were suddenly disrupted. Several works have discussed the potential for terrorism to intentionally target ESS technology as part of a larger kinetic attack. Despite this, the resilience of first responder agencies to technological disruption and their preparedness for such an attack has largely remained unexplored. To bridge this gap, we implemented a novel scenario-based interview methodology involving senior officials from emergency service agencies across the United States. These interviews explored how each agency prepared for a disruption of operational technology and what factors might influence different levels of preparation between them. Participants were asked to describe their responses to a hypothetical scenario modeled after historical cyber-attacks against ESS infrastructure. The results indicate that while ESS agencies are prepared for short-term technological disruptions, they are likely to struggle with long-term or hybrid incidents. The data further revealed that agencies often lack dedicated expertise in cybersecurity, technology, and emergency management that could otherwise elevate resilience to interruptions of operational technology. These findings emphasize the need for investment in redundant analog systems, increased training for frontline personnel, and a focused effort against loss of specialized technical expertise among ESS agencies.

title: TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin of Telegram Crisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-Powered Information Operations
summary: Large language models make it cheap to run influence operations whose messages never repeat, yet real platforms offer almost no ground truth for testing whether coordination detectors can find them. The problem is sharpest on Telegram, which moderates little and spreads content through broadcast channels and forwarding rather than a follow graph. We introduce TeleTwin, an LLM-powered digital twin of a Telegram crisis-discourse ecosystem in which channels are agents, each instantiated from the history of a real channel, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 public channels on the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflict (March-August 2025). On a held-out period containing the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, the twin tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 against 0.64) and reacts to the war unprompted, but it over-focuses on the conflict, over-amplifies forwarding cascades, underestimates the shock and writes recognisably LLM-like text. We then inject LLM-written campaigns with known membership into the real data and into the twin. In real data, identical-text, co-URL and synchrony detectors fail once a campaign rewords, staggers or drops links; multilingual semantic similarity recovers loud campaigns, including cross-lingual ones, but not quiet ones, and its false positives fall unevenly across political perspectives. Inside the twin all detectors fail, because the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than the real one. Digital twins can supply ground truth for campaigns, but not, without calibrating their diversity, a realistic background for evaluating semantic detectors.

title: Hidden urban exposure to energy-price shocks: spreading burdens and shifting hotspots
summary: Cities need to anticipate where energy-price shocks could intensify hardship beyond established hotspots. How income distributions and fuel-price balances jointly shape this hidden exposure remains unclear. Here we address this gap by stress-testing nearly one million properties in six English local authorities, combining required-energy costs for existing housing with modelled local income distributions. Under gas-led crisis prices, 41% of neighbourhoods in the highest local exposure quarter lie outside the highest official fuel-poverty quarter. Electricity-led stress changes this hidden geography: when electricity unit prices alone triple from 2021, comparable to the unmitigated late-2022 cap increase, 38% of the resulting hidden-exposure group are absent from the crisis-based group. Entering neighbourhoods have newer, more efficient housing, more flats and greater electricity dependence than retained areas. Crisis preparedness should extend household protection beyond current hardship hotspots, using fuel-specific stress tests to anticipate support needs as fuel prices and heating systems change.

title: CARVS: A Congestion-Aware Algorithm for Online Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery in Human-Collaborative Warehouses
summary: Intelligent warehouse systems have transformed logistics by integrating robots with minimal infrastructure changes, boosting efficiency and optimizing workflows compared to traditional human-only operations. However, human-robot collaboration introduces new challenges, particularly due to human uncertainty, which leads to dynamic interactions and unpredictable behavior. To address these complexities, this paper presents the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery with Human Collaboration (MAPDwHC) problem, an extension of the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery (MAPD) problem that incorporates human unpredictability. This problem adds key constraints, such as dynamic obstacles caused by robots temporarily blocking paths when interacting with humans, and the need for real-time responsiveness. We formalize the MAPDwHC problem with additional constraints and properties. Based on this problem setting, we propose the CARVS algorithm, which improves task assignment and path planning by integrating task swapping, validation checks, and random initialization. CARVS reduces congestion, enhances adaptability to human-robot interactions, and ensures real-time responsiveness. Simulation results show that CARVS significantly reduces timeouts of path planning in large-scale scenarios where traditional MAPD algorithms fail, improving both efficiency and scalability.

title: Navigating Deception on Gay Dating Apps: A Qualitative Study of Users' Experiences, Verification Strategies, and Community Knowledge in China
summary: Gay dating applications have become essential platforms for sexual minority men to seek relationships, intimacy, and community, yet they also expose users to a range of deceptive interactions that remain underexplored in HCI and CSCW research. This study examines how gay male users in China experience, identify, and respond to deception on dating applications. Through semi-structured interviews with 22 participants who used platforms such as Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul, we identify a typology of deceptive practices that users encounter, including relational misrepresentation for sexual access, sustained emotional deception, financial fraud, marketing behavior disguised as ordinary users, and false identity construction. We further analyze the verification and coping strategies that users develop through long-term platform use, such as judging relational intent through interactional pace, identifying financial risk signals, recognizing commercial promotion accounts, and progressively verifying identity authenticity. Finally, we show that risk recognition is not merely an individual capacity but a collaborative practice that gradually emerges through the circulation of experience within the community, the summarization of recurrent deceptive tactics, and the learning of shared rules. Our findings contribute to CSCW scholarship by demonstrating how users of a marginalized community collectively construct practical knowledge about deception, and by revealing that trust assessment on dating platforms operates as a layered, probabilistic, and socially distributed process rather than a binary judgment.

title: Duration-Aware Dissimilarity in Temporal Networks
summary:
Temporal-network comparison becomes substantially more challenging when interactions are associated with explicit traversal times, since both event timing and duration determine temporal reachability and journey performance. We introduce a duration-aware dissimilarity framework for temporal networks whose edges carry departure times and traversal durations. The proposed approach compares networks through source-specific temporal-distance profiles using the $1$-Wasserstein distance, thereby retaining both temporal information and source correspondence.
  We evaluate the framework on real public-transport timetable networks under controlled schedule delays, duration-aware randomized reference models, and naturally occurring temporal variations. We further benchmark the proposed measure against existing path-based temporal dissimilarity approaches under the same perturbation scenarios. The results show that the proposed representation responds consistently to both the extent and the magnitude of temporal disruption, while retaining distinctions that may be compressed by contact- or hop-based temporal summaries. Overall, the findings support duration-aware temporal distances as a useful basis for comparing temporal systems in which traversal and waiting times directly affect network performance.

title: Fabric retrofit scenario analysis under uncertainty for an urban housing stock using machine learning
summary: Fabric retrofit is central to decarbonising housing, and planning it depends on expected savings and their uncertainty. This study asks which upgrade saves most per dwelling and across a housing portfolio, how uncertain the savings are, and whether upgrade order matters. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that converts predicted changes in energy performance certificate scores after wall, roof and window upgrades into standardised energy-cost savings and emission reductions. Six machine-learning models predict the 1-100 Standard Assessment Procedure (SAP) energy-cost and environmental impact (EI) emission scores from 17 certificate descriptors. Each model's errors on similar dwellings give calibrated prediction intervals. A global-best strategy applies the most accurate model throughout; a sample-specific strategy chooses each dwelling's model using these local errors. The analysis covers 103,414 officially registered dwellings in Westminster, London. CatBoost was the global-best model, with mean absolute errors of 3.487 SAP and 4.379 EI points on held-out dwellings. Both strategies projected similar savings; under global-best, roof insulation saved most per dwelling, GBP 203 annually (uncertainty range 176-229), and wall insulation most across the portfolio, GBP 6.09 million annually (uncertainty range 5.69-6.72). For 5,382 dwellings needing all three upgrades, every order delivered the same final package, yet installing roofs, walls, then windows a year apart accumulated 54% more projected cost savings over three years than the reverse order. Emission reductions followed the same pattern. Using only certificate data, the framework helps local authorities rank measures for dwellings and portfolios and sequence upgrades to bring savings forward.

title: Measuring Consensus in AI Agent Networks
comment: 4 pages. Accepted at the NANDA Workshop, IEEE TPS-ISA 2026
summary: As AI agents become increasingly connected through networks and take on tasks that require negotiation and joint decision-making, a systematic approach is needed to assess how their views converge and what information supports their decisions. We present an evaluation framework that treats consensus formation as the evolution of publicly stated positions toward a shared region, using accumulated communication history as context. The framework tracks position trajectories, group dispersion, and information expressed in public messages. Two case studies examine staffing decisions based on distributed facts and decisions requiring agents to reconcile duplicate information and a cancelled contract. Results from 1,872 completed runs associate sharing explanations with more accurate group decisions, while the second task reveals persistent disagreement despite accurate aggregate answers. Membership-change experiments provide a complementary evaluation. By separating convergence among agents from progress toward a task's full-information answer, the framework relates decision accuracy and bounded disagreement to the information available during the exchange.

title: You Already Have Me--Why Do You Still Use Blued?'' How Gay Dating Apps Shape Intimate Relationships Among Chinese Gay Men
summary: Gay dating applications such as Blued are widely used for meeting partners, yet their role does not end once an intimate relationship is formed. When these platforms persist within an established relationship, they transform from matchmaking tools into a form of relational infrastructure that both partners must continuously manage. Building on existing CSCW and HCI research that has primarily examined how social media triggers jealousy, surveillance, or trust issues in intimate relationships, this study investigates how the persistent presence of gay dating applications shapes the dynamics of intimate relationships among Chinese gay men. Through semi-structured interviews with 23 self-identified gay men aged 19 to 55, we identify a recurring cyclical process: platform signals-such as online status, profile updates, distance indicators, and usage records-trigger suspicion and conflict; partners invest negotiation labor through intent explanation, visibility control, rule formation, or silence; and these negotiations eventually sediment into temporary governance settlements that reduce trigger frequency but remain conditionally stable. We identify four types of governance settlements: infrastructure removal, transparency governance, silence agreements, and layered/open agreements. Each settlement addresses the governance problems of platform presence, visibility distribution, and loyalty boundaries differently, yet none achieves permanent stability due to platforms' reversible entry mechanisms and continuous visibility cues. Our findings extend existing CSCW research on digital technology and intimate relationships by revealing a more complex process than previously documented: platform signals not only trigger emotional responses but prompt partners to engage in sustained relational negotiation through explanation, visibility management, rule formation, or silence.

title: Modeling Group Socialization in Online Communities
summary: Newcomers to online communities must learn a group's norms to participate successfully. This process is known as socialization, and has been the subject of considerable study in the online communities literature. Foundational work on group socialization in social psychology, however, suggests that socialization is actually a bidirectional process: individuals and communities adapt to each other's needs. In this work we develop a formal quantitative model of socialization, and present the first large scale empirical validation of the bidirectional socialization hypothesis using Reddit data. More specifically, we focus on linguistic socialization, and model users' comments in online communities as a mixture of in-group language and language from ``background'' communities they previously participated in. On a dataset of 112 subreddits (7.8 million tokens) find that our bidirectional model makes predictions that better generalize across users and time than two unidirectional socialization models. Furthermore, we conduct a qualitative analysis in which we demonstrate that our model is able to extract interpretable socialization patterns from the data that align with the existing literature. Specifically our model is able to learn that users conform more to group norms in topically niche communities with stricter content moderation rules, and that long time users conform more than newcomers. We emphasize that the claims made in this paper are explicitly falsifiable -- we are staking out a clear claim about what the socialization process looks like, and encourage future work to challenge our model.

title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
summary: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

title: AgentSoV: Virtual Sensing for LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Stream of Variation
summary: Large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems (MASs) solve complex tasks through interacting agents, yet their reliability is difficult to analyze because failures depend on both individual agents and how information and errors propagate across the system. Existing approaches largely treat this as post-hoc failure attribution, but do not provide a common model across heterogeneous MAS architectures or support broader analysis of information influence and observability. We introduce AgentSoV, a virtual-sensing framework that models MAS execution as a stochastic dynamic system through Stream of Variation (SoV). AgentSoV maps heterogeneous trajectories into diagnostic stages, constructs virtual measurements from observable outputs, and learns cross-stage variation propagation with a state-space model. Its representation is architecture-aware in stage dependencies yet architecture-agnostic in analytical language, supporting chain-structured, orchestration-based, and directed acyclic graph (DAG)-structured MASs. Without re-executing the MAS, AgentSoV supports three system-level analyses: failure attribution identifies where abnormal variation enters; stage-input influence quantifies how strongly intermediate inputs affect downstream outcomes; and virtual-sensor placement selects complementary observations under a monitoring budget. Experiments across multiple MAS architectures demonstrate a unified approach to fault localization, information influence, and observability. AgentSoV reframes agentic execution as a dynamic system to model rather than merely text to inspect, providing insights for MAS structure and component design.

title: Trinketry: Materializing Elements to Anchor Traceable Design Histories
summary: Generative tools enable visual designers to rapidly explore diverse design directions---but as flawed generated outputs proliferate, designers may lose track of promising ideas and the context of their development. We introduce trinkets: user-preserved design elements that function as reusable materials, retrieval queries, and navigational anchors for tracing how ideas emerge, transform, and recur throughout design history. We implement this concept in Trinketry, a visual exploration canvas. In a within-subjects study with 12 concept designers, Trinketry supported focused element-level exploration and greater perceived control than a simple branching image generation history baseline. A follow-up study with six returning designers examined delayed design history sensemaking, continuation of work, and reconstruction of others' processes. Compared with whole-image histories, Trinketry supported more precise reconstruction of process structure, turning points, and goals, while helping designers recover overlooked materials and continue exploration. However, opportunities remain to augment trace representations with explicit statements of design rationale.

title: Source Attribution and Audience Uptake in Digital Witnessing: Evidence from a Chinese Diaspora Account on X
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-60), 2027
summary: Digital-witnessing research explains how citizen testimony becomes publicly visible. Less is known about audience uptake after publication and whether the attributed source corresponds to the form of response. This study analyzes 47,635 posts (April 2022 to May 2026) from Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher, a diaspora-based account that curates and publishes reports and testimony from inside China for transnational audiences. Among 25,093 witness-relevant posts, 3,601 explicitly attribute their material to ordinary submitters. These posts receive more replies than other witness-relevant posts across adjusted analyses and show a more reply-oriented profile. The primary doubly robust retweet estimate is near zero. Among audited replies to November 2022 user-submitted posts, 91.4% substantively engage the focal material. The pattern is consistent with ordinary-person source attribution presenting testimony as situated and open to public response. The study extends digital witnessing beyond visibility by separating redistribution from the public response that gathers around testimony.

title: Modeling the Coevolution of Human Skills and AI Adoption
summary: The value of relying on generative AI depends on two quantities that evolve with its use: users' unaided skill, which may decline without practice, and the originality of AI-assisted work, which may decline as more people rely on similar tools. We model this process as a coevolutionary game in which individuals choose between autonomous and AI-assisted work, with autonomous practice strengthening their skills while reliance on AI gradually erodes them. When the reinforcing effect of skill erosion outweighs the crowding cost of lost originality, the population exhibits two alternative stable states: low AI adoption with high average skill, and high AI adoption with low average skill. Because skill is individual, autonomous workers remain more skilled than AI users, making autonomous work less vulnerable to population-wide skill decline. The strength of this effect is governed by a timescale ratio: the rate at which skills adapt relative to the rate at which individuals change strategy. The same ratio determines the full distribution of skills, which we derive analytically. Populations with identical AI adoption and average skill can differ sharply: when strategies change frequently, skills remain homogeneous and collective lock-in to high AI adoption is stronger; when strategies persist, lock-in weakens but the population can polarize into highly skilled autonomous workers and AI-dependent individuals. Modeling output overlap further shows that more diverse AI outputs can make widespread adoption harder to reverse. Together, these results expose tradeoffs between the benefits of widespread AI adoption and its long-run risks, making collective lock-in and skill polarization distinct intervention targets.

We entered the GLEE competition in its final week with one protected agent, Milton, and four instrument agents that ran deterministic, per-game randomized trials of policy changes; Milton received changes only through pre-specified gates or registered, rollback-guarded production rules. In negotiation, learned pricing improves adjusted percentile by 0.071 (n=21,168); in bargaining, a continuation model conditioned on the rejected offer did not improve on a recency-weighted incumbent and was retired. In persuasion, a preregistered five-dose experiment (7,391 assigned games, blinded until a fixed stop) shows that recommending every unit raises sales by 0.194 of the maximum (95% CI [0.147, 0.241]) where the receiver's slack makes obedience rational (52% of the Bayesian benchmark), lowers them where it does not (-0.067), and produces a larger early-to-late purchase decline than honest recommendations (-0.123). title: Usability, User Experience, and Acceptability of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality in Younger and Older Adults
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables, supplementary material are included
summary: Immersive virtual reality (VR) adaptations of neuropsychological tests change how a test operates. Before their scores are interpreted, the individuals they are intended to assess should find them usable, acceptable and tolerable, and for older adults this evidence is usually missing. This study evaluated the experience of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze adaptation of the Trail Making Test that requires no hand-held controller, in 47 younger (20-38 years) and 44 older adults (64-81 years). After the task, participants rated usability, pragmatic and hedonic user experience, acceptability, and cybersickness. The study had three aims: to compare the two age groups on these ratings; to examine whether the ratings were associated with age group, gaming and technology experience, and whether cybersickness was associated with motion sickness susceptibility; and to examine whether the ratings were related to TMT-VR completion and error-adjusted times. Both groups rated the TMT-VR as highly usable, acceptable and pleasant to use. Older adults gave slightly lower usability and pragmatic ratings, but neither the age-group differences nor the associations with age group or previous experience were statistically significant after correction. Cybersickness was low, with 38 of the 91 participants reporting no symptoms; it did not differ between the age groups and was not associated with motion sickness susceptibility. No correlation between the ratings and TMT-VR performance survived correction. The TMT-VR with head-gaze selection is therefore usable, acceptable and well tolerated by older as well as younger adults. Because the ratings were favourable across the whole range of TMT-VR scores, slower or less accurate performance is unlikely to reflect difficulty with the interface.

title: YouTube Clips and Broad but Shallow Attention to Candidates: Evidence from the 2024 Tokyo Gubernatorial Election
summary: Video-sharing platforms and social media have gained influence in election campaigns, and third-party edited videos (called kirinuki in Japanese; hereafter, "clip videos") in particular have attracted attention. In Japan, Shinji Ishimaru, previously unknown nationally, finished second in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, a result widely attributed to his popularity on YouTube. Focusing on this case, we analyzed 44,331 YouTube videos relating to the nine leading candidates, posted between July 5, 2020, and July 7, 2024. Using cumulative views and engagement data as of June 25, 2025, we examined the relationship between clip videos and the attention candidates received. Regression analyses with standard errors clustered by channel showed that Ishimaru, the most watched candidate, did not draw the most active engagement. Videos mentioning Ishimaru received about 36% fewer likes and 41% fewer comments at the same number of views, whereas some candidates with fewer views recorded higher engagement rates. Clip videos were associated with this breadth of attention. They received about 1.8 times more views but 26% fewer comments at the same number of views, and mentions of Ishimaru were associated with about 2.6 times more views among non-clip videos. The interaction between the two, however, was not significant, and understanding the prominence of Ishimaru's cumulative views requires considering both the number of clip videos about him and the views per video. These results suggest that the spread of attention through clip videos may have functioned as a broad but shallow pathway, distinct from the formation of committed support.

title: A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
comment: 48 pages, 19 figures (10 main + 9 SI), 2 tables, Code and data: https://github.com/galenwilkerson/collective-foraging-cascades

title: Learning Who Talks to Whom: Role-Aware Communication Topology Scheduling for Efficient LLM Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent systems driven by large language models (LLMs) rely on structured communication topologies to facilitate information exchange and collaborative reasoning. However, effectively scheduling these topologies to dynamically determine who talks to whom and when to communicate remains a fundamental challenge in balancing collective reasoning performance against exponential token overhead. Existing topology scheduling approaches either enforce static communication graphs that cannot adapt to dynamic problem-solving states, or overlook agent role complementarity while failing to explicitly incorporate the synthesized graph structure into team-level decision evaluation. To tackle these limitations, we propose ACTS, a role-aware adaptive communication topology scheduling framework for efficient LLM multi-agent collaboration. Orchestrated within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, ACTS introduces a novel dual-attention mechanism. Specifically, a Role-conditioned Relational Attention module dynamically selects variable-cardinality interaction partners based on agent roles and evolving execution states, while a Topological Attention Mixer explicitly embeds the directed communication topology into team value decomposition for precise credit assignment. Comprehensive evaluations across 9 challenging benchmarks covering code generation, multi-step reasoning, general knowledge, and competitive mathematics demonstrate that ACTS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, boosting average accuracy by up to 6.19 percentage points while reducing token consumption by over 15%. The project website is available at https://acts-mas.github.io/ACTS/.

title: Indirect Influences of Artificial Intelligence Advice on Complex Sepsis Treatment Decisions
summary: Sepsis is a major public health concern, and many sepsis patients die due to ineffective hemodynamic management. Artificial intelligence could support hemodynamic decisions, particularly in complex cases where conflicting information and comorbidities drive uncertainty and practice variation. However, these systems' real-world value depends on not just accuracy, but how they influence the quality of clinician decisions. We first retrospectively evaluated an AI system's recommendations in 6,928 sepsis patients, finding that they improved upon the original providers' decisions overall but had significantly worse performance in complex cases. We then conducted a pre-registered experiment with 228 US critical care physicians to test their use of this imperfect advice in six complex treatment decisions, using one of three advice types designed to vary reasoning autonomy. Participants given simple model recommendations overcame poor advice, choosing optimal treatments in 56.3% of decisions compared to 31.8% if they had always followed the recommendations. They also made significantly better decisions than those receiving a less prescriptive advice type (42.9%). Physicians selectively adapted and improved weak advice, likely because it prompted them to reconsider their assessment. Our findings suggest that improving sepsis care decisions with AI may require accounting for these indirect influences resulting from human-AI collaborative reasoning.

title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
summary: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.

title: Negative partisanship drives anti-frontrunner volatility in election dynamics
summary: Negative partisanship---where voter mobilization is driven primarily by aversion toward an opposing candidate rather than positive alignment---profoundly reshapes modern electoral dynamics. Here, we formulate a two-dimensional piecewise map to model campaign opinion dynamics, where voter abstention arises endogenously from a latent spectrum of voter activation barriers. We show that cross-candidate rejection sensitivity triggers a non-smooth collapse of abstention, dividing the phase space into an under-mobilized regime and a fully mobilized campaign regime. In symmetric elections with radicalized voter bases, spontaneous symmetry breaking via a pitchfork bifurcation gives rise to asymmetric polling attractors partitioned by mirror-symmetric basins of attraction, where early public perceptions---encoded in initial campaign conditions---act as a deterministic catalyst selecting candidate lead lock-in long before election day. For elevated cross-rejection, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes via a period-doubling flip bifurcation, driving persistent anti-frontrunner polling swings. Rather than predicting static candidate hegemony, our model reveals that high negative partisanship turns elections into time-sensitive dynamical systems, where final election outcomes reflect discrete sampling snapshots of an oscillating campaign trajectory.

title: Behavioral Probes for Information Flow in LLM Swarms
summary: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.

title: GazeAgent: VLM-Guided Implicit Gaze Calibration from Egocentric Multimodal Behavior for AI Glasses
summary: AI glasses typically require explicit, user-specific eye-tracker calibration, and accuracy can drift when the device shifts during use. We present GazeAgent, a VLM-guided framework that continuously and adaptively improves gaze-calibration accuracy from naturally occurring behavior without asking users to interrupt their activities. GazeAgent identifies precise visual attention (PVA) events from multimodal streams of inertial measurement unit (IMU), gaze, and wearer-hand signals, validates their task relevance, and localizes functional targets as pseudo-calibration targets. In a 10-participant scripted study, the system detected all 820 predefined PVA opportunities and, under device disturbance, reduced median gaze error by 44.1% compared with explicit calibration. In a five-participant case study, autonomous calibration produced the lowest workload and interruption ratings, and all participants preferred it for routine use. By deriving task-critical targets from natural multimodal behavior, GazeAgent demonstrates the potential for continuous, adaptive, and low-burden gaze interaction on egocentric AI glasses.

title: A Theoretical Perspective on Link Prediction Heuristics
summary: In network analysis, nodes with different degrees are usually weighted differently in tasks such as link prediction. For example, two individuals connected to the same high-degree node (e.g., a celebrity) are often considered less likely to know each other than if they share a low-degree connection. In this paper, we theoretically justify the reasoning behind this heuristic using a graph generation model. In this model, nodes are embedded in a latent metric space, and edges are more likely to form between nearby nodes. We analytically derive degree-based weighting schemes for commonly used link prediction and similarity measures. In particular, we identify the optimal weighting scheme for the Common Neighbors index and extend our analysis to other popular heuristics, including the graph distance. Our theoretical findings align with previous empirical observations, and we further validate them through experiments on both synthetic and real-world networks.

title: Pairwise assessment correlations predict cooperation of the Leading Eight under private assessment
summary: Indirect reciprocity can sustain cooperation when individuals use reputations to decide whom to help. The Leading Eight norms sustain such cooperation under public assessment, where all individuals share the same assessments. Under private assessment, however, observers may disagree, yet their assessments remain correlated. Two quantities, the average fraction of good assessments $h$ and the conditional probability $h_{\mathrm G}$ that one observer assesses a player as good given that another does, are known to determine the stability of cooperation, but how $h_{\mathrm G}$ itself is determined has remained open. Within a pairwise approximation, we derive a closed equation for $h_{\mathrm G}$ that, together with that for $h$, determines both quantities for all eight norms, including third-order ones. This description substantially improves agreement with simulations over a mean-field approximation that neglects correlations, and recovers the known classification of the Leading Eight into three classes. The remaining discrepancies are largest for L2 and L5 at low error rates and decrease as assessment error increases. Relating $h_{\mathrm G}$ to the variance of individual goodness suggests that these discrepancies reflect information beyond the first two moments of the goodness distribution. Our framework provides a concise and analytically tractable tool for evaluating social norms under private assessment.

title: Discovery-Probability Graph Planning for Embodied Agents in Tasks with Hidden Cooperation Requirements
summary: Embodied agents are increasingly capable of perceiving, planning, and acting autonomously in dynamic environments, demonstrating strong performance on complex cooperative tasks. Recent advances typically assume that cooperative tasks are known in advance. In real-world applications, however, hidden-cooperation tasks are more common: the need for cooperation only becomes apparent after an agent observes and interacts with task-related targets. In this paper, we first present HiddenCoop, a benchmark for effectively evaluating agent cooperation in hidden-cooperation tasks. We further propose Discovery-Probability Graph Planning (DPGP), a method for enabling effective agent cooperation in such tasks. At the core of DPGP is a discovery-probability graph that encodes the probability distribution over the number and locations of task-related targets, facilitating effective and efficient information exchange among agents. A search algorithm is then used to derive action plans that minimize expected costs. Experiments show that DPGP achieves cooperative-task success rates of 99.3% on C-WAH and 58.3% on TDW-MAT, surpassing all compared baselines, while also reducing overall embodied execution time and substantially lowering LLM token usage. Our code is available at https://github.com/hnu-vis/DPGP.

title: From Neglect to Resignation: Understanding the Evolution of Mobile Privacy
summary: This decade-long longitudinal qualitative study follows 31 smartphone users in China across four interview waves (2014-2023) to examine how mobile privacy understanding evolves alongside shifting computing infrastructures. Findings reveal three stages shaped by distinct interactional mechanisms: early functional acceptance of permission-based data access, growing vigilance triggered by behavioral tracking feedback loops, and eventual resignation as AI-driven inference made ecosystem-level profiling feel inescapable. Rather than a stable attitude, digital resignation emerges through cumulative infrastructure exposure, as each new system layer retroactively reinterpreted earlier permissions and exhausted users' capacity for self-management. The study challenges permission-centric design assumptions and proposes inference visibility, context isolation, and automated privacy agency as system-level responses.

title: Optimizing Marketing Budgets for Social Influence: A Generalized Fractional Incentives Framework
summary: Marketing managers routinely allocate limited budgets across individuals in social networks whose responsiveness and influence vary substantially. We study the problem of Budgeted Generalized Fractional Influence Maximization (BGFIM), which captures the allocation of continuous levels of marketing spend across users in the presence of heterogeneous response and network spillovers. In this framework, adoption probabilities are governed by user-specific response functions that capture both baseline propensity and marginal responsiveness, while incentive costs vary across users. We propose a scalable solution approach based on a discrete greedy procedure with provable approximation guarantees, enabling tractable optimization under realistic budget constraints. Our formulation generalizes prior influence maximization models by allowing heterogeneous response and cost structures, providing a more flexible representation of targeted marketing interventions. Using experiments on multiple large-scale networks, we show that continuous allocation strategies can outperform standard heuristics and improve influence outcomes under heterogeneous conditions, and we illustrate how the framework can support profit-oriented decision making by identifying budget levels that balance marginal returns and costs. Overall, our results highlight the value of fine-grained budget allocation in networked marketing environments and offer a scalable approach for data-driven marketing resource allocation.

title: Higher-Order Co-Infection on Hypergraphs
summary: People encounter infections through overlapping groups, such as households, classrooms, and workplaces. Understanding how these shared contacts affect the spread of multiple pathogens is critical to determining what information epidemic models need to retain. We introduce HyCo-SIS (Higher-order Co-infection SIS), a discrete-time SIS model on hypergraphs with explicit reinforcement between overlapping active groups and pairwise transmission. We investigate how this reinforcement affects infection dynamics and whether simplified representations of hypergraphs preserve the resulting behavior. We derive an exact representation of overlap reinforcement as target-dependent four-person interactions and determine when a symmetric representation is possible. Numerical experiments examine reinforcement strength, contact structure, and susceptibility to secondary infection, as well as calibrated pairwise approximations. Our results demonstrate that redistributing overlap weights can substantially change finite-time co-infection even when every individual's total overlap coefficient is preserved. We further derive an exact five-person calculation and demonstrate why equal mean infection pressure does not necessarily produce equal acquisition probabilities. These findings identify how the allocation of higher-order interactions can influence contagion dynamics beyond their aggregate strength. Beyond epidemiology, this work contributes to the statistical physics of spreading processes by examining how the arrangement of many-body interactions shapes collective dynamics, and what information is lost when those interactions are simplified.

title: TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin of Telegram Crisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-Powered Information Operations
summary: Large language models make it cheap to run influence operations whose messages never repeat, yet real platforms offer almost no ground truth for testing whether coordination detectors can find them. The problem is sharpest on Telegram, which moderates little and spreads content through broadcast channels and forwarding rather than a follow graph. We introduce TeleTwin, an LLM-powered digital twin of a Telegram crisis-discourse ecosystem in which channels are agents, each instantiated from the history of a real channel, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 public channels on the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflict (March-August 2025). On a held-out period containing the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, the twin tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 against 0.64) and reacts to the war unprompted, but it over-focuses on the conflict, over-amplifies forwarding cascades, underestimates the shock and writes recognisably LLM-like text. We then inject LLM-written campaigns with known membership into the real data and into the twin. In real data, identical-text, co-URL and synchrony detectors fail once a campaign rewords, staggers or drops links; multilingual semantic similarity recovers loud campaigns, including cross-lingual ones, but not quiet ones, and its false positives fall unevenly across political perspectives. Inside the twin all detectors fail, because the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than the real one. Digital twins can supply ground truth for campaigns, but not, without calibrating their diversity, a realistic background for evaluating semantic detectors.

title: Say It or Grab It? Conversational Control of UI Adaptations in Mixed Reality
summary: Mixed reality interfaces must continuously adapt to a user's changing task and environment, yet adaptation policies are fixed in advance, either preset by the system or configured by the user. Natural language offers a way to state changing needs mid-task, but whether users can express interface behavior this way, and what it gains over direct manipulation, is unknown. We first elicited how users verbalize adaptation needs (N=19). We then built ConverseMR, which translates a spoken request into adaptation objectives and constraints and satisfies them continuously as the user's context changes. In a within-subjects study (N=24), conversational and direct control proved complementary: direct manipulation for precision, ConverseMR for reach and expressive breadth, with their combination rated highest. Spoken commands were rarely final and users frequently refined and replaced them upon experiencing the result, characteristic of, what we call, user-led adaptation, where users communicate adaption needs and the system identifies a solution.

title: Where Does Rhetorical Distortion Live? A Multi-Platform, Multi-Language Measurement of Influencer Content
summary: Much of the manipulation in online influencer content is not false but disproportionate: an accurate fact is framed as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Fact-checking and clickbait detection are not designed to capture such framing, and little is known about where it originates: with the creator, the topic, the platform, or the audience that replies. We operationalize rhetorical distortion through five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion) and measure it with a three-tier pipeline in which bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false-positive contexts, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. Applying the pipeline to 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms (RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter), we find that platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (Kruskal-Wallis $\varepsilon^2=0.33$; two-way ANOVA $η_p^2=0.49$ for platform vs. $0.09$ for category). X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). Classifying tweets and their replies separately shows where this comes from: the reply layer readers see under a post (its top-5 replies) carries 3.5x the distortion of the tweet it answers (7.65 vs. 2.17, $p<10^{-6}$, 36 of 43 accounts), driven by Loaded Language. At equal text length the gap shrinks to 1.5x but remains significant, and creator tweets alone are statistically indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky. Two independent human annotators confirm the reply gap, and the platform ordering and the reply gap replicate with GPT-4o as a second classifier. On threaded platforms, measured distortion thus lives largely in the audience layer, which motivates measurement that separates creator and reply text.

title: Systemic collapse emergence from climate-induced perturbations in transportation networks
summary: The interaction between human infrastructures and external events results in loss of functionality or even complete system disruption through a snowball effect of cascading-failures. Their complex interplay challenges their prevention, affecting the human population that rely on their functionality. Understanding how these networks respond to external perturbations is crucial for predicting and mitigating the impacts of disruptive events. In particular, meteorological events, while not preventable, can have significant impacts on human infrastructure. Here, we propose a model coupling the dynamics of transportation systems to the dynamics of external events considered as fields, to capture at the same time the critical behavior of the former and the level of influence of the latter. The impact of rainfalls on real-world railway networks provides a compelling case study, showcasing local endemic and system-wide disruptions around a critical value of the rainfall strength. Remarkably, localized perturbations on the wider network reveals the local weaknesses of the global infrastructure, and we assess them in terms of system perturbability and corresponding societal risk. Our framework opens the door to the quantitative analysis of criticalities in essential human infrastructure imputable to vulnerabilities that are set to intensify due to climate change.

title: Collaborative Hand Drawing to Conceptualize Usable Privacy and Security Research Problems: Students' Perspectives (Extended Version)
comment: This document is the authors' extended preprint for a short paper in the proceedings of Koli Calling'26, ACM (DOI: 10.1145/3856208.3856277)
summary: In this paper, we explore students' perspectives on incorporating hand drawing to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems. We surveyed 64 female students who participated in an in-class collaborative hand drawing activity to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems as part of a group-based student research project on usable privacy and security in an information and computer security course for undergraduate students. Our survey responses suggest that students perceived the drawing exercise positively. That is, they found it helpful in several aspects, enjoyable, and they recommend it to other students taking the course. The students also said that they would like to have such an exercise in other courses, such as Principles of Human-Computer Interaction and Fundamentals of Data Networks. Only three students mentioned downsides of the exercise, namely doubts about their drawing skills. Our results provide useful insights for educators seeking to enhance the student learning experience.

title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
summary: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

title: Constrained modularity maximization in complex networks via branch-and-price
summary: Modularity maximization is widely used to identify community structure in complex networks. In many applications, however, community detection must also incorporate prior knowledge and domain-specific requirements beyond network topology. We study constrained modularity maximization with restrictions on the number of communities, must-link and cannot-link relations, and general resource constraints. While fast heuristics can provide high-quality solutions, they generally lack optimality guarantees, whereas exact mathematical-programming approaches can become computationally demanding as the network size and constraint complexity increase. We develop a unified optimization framework offering complementary heuristic and exact solution methods. These include a constrained Louvain heuristic for feasible solution generation, a column-generation heuristic with graph-partitioning-based pricing, and exact branch-and-price algorithms using mixed-integer linear programming and sparse mixed-integer quadratic programming formulations for the pricing subproblem. We develop a cutting-plane procedure providing independent upper bounds to assess solution quality when exact optimization cannot be completed. Experiments on 11 unconstrained networks with up to 1,005 nodes and 30 constrained instances with up to 379 nodes demonstrate the complementary roles of these methods. The column-generation heuristic rapidly improves the constrained Louvain solutions across the tested constraint classes, while branch-and-price using the sparse quadratic formulation solves 29 of the 30 constrained instances to optimality within a one-hour time limit. This formulation becomes particularly effective on larger, sparse, undirected networks by substantially reducing the size of the exact pricing model. Overall, the framework guides method selection to balance computational time, solution quality, and optimality guarantees.

title: Leveraging Mental Models for Human-Centered Explanations: A Systematic Design Approach Illustrated by Explainable Fake Review Identification
comment: 38 pages, 10 figures, 8 tables. Keywords: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Human-centered AI; Mental models; Fake review detection; User-centered explanation design; Natural language explanations; Cognitive heuristics
summary: Explainable AI (XAI) often prioritizes model fidelity over user intelligibility, yielding explanations that satisfy technical transparency yet fail to support human sense-making. We propose a human-centered approach, MIND-X (Mental-model INtegrated Design for eXplainability), which aligns explanations with users' mental models, commonsense concepts, and judgment heuristics. Using fake review detection as a case study, we contribute: (1) a qualitative study (n=10) that elicits how people assess review credibility and produces an actionable, design-guiding taxonomy of perceptual cues; (2) a set of design principles that link those cues to explanation strategies and prompt LLMs to generate adaptive, language-based explanations; and (3) a quantitative evaluation (n=166) showing that these explanations offer distinct advantages over token-level transparency methods widely used in explainable text classification in terms of understandability, satisfaction, perceived trust, persuasiveness, and decision-making support. Rather than claiming general superiority, our evaluation illustrates how grounding explanations in users' everyday reasoning practices can produce more intelligible and context-sensitive accounts. Our findings advance human-centered explanation design beyond a mere "gloss of transparency," demonstrating that a mental-model-aligned design process can improve intelligibility and support accountability across user-centered explanation tasks.
